concepts.title: Matter Is Made of Particles and Atoms
concepts.definition: Everything felt around us is matter, and matter consists of tiny particles; pushing deeper, the particles of substances are built from atoms - the microscopic world inside matter begins at the atom.
concepts.key_idea: Zoom from objects to particles to atoms: the journey of structure goes inward.
concepts.textbook_ref: iesc108.txt opening sections (matter and its particles)
question_patterns: what is matter composed of - explain the particle idea
define an atom in your own words
how do the particles of matter relate to atoms
give evidence that matter is particulate
what does the journey inside the atom mean
arrange in increasing size: object, molecule, atom

solution_steps.explain: Every object is built from its tiny particles.
Molecules break into atoms, the chemical building blocks.
Atoms themselves hold smaller particles inside.

concepts.title: Subatomic Particles: Electron, Proton and Neutron
concepts.definition: Inside the atom sit three key subatomic particles: negatively charged electrons, positively charged protons and neutral neutrons; the protons and neutrons crowd into a tiny central nucleus while electrons occupy the space around it.
concepts.key_idea: Electrons outside, protons and neutrons inside: charge and mass divide the labour.
concepts.textbook_ref: iesc108.txt sections on discovery and properties of subatomic particles
question_patterns: name the three subatomic particles with their charges
where are protons and neutrons located in an atom
which particle carries a negative charge and who discovered it
compare the masses of the three subatomic particles
what makes an atom electrically neutral
identify the particle from the given property

solution_steps.explain: Electron, proton, neutron with charges -1, +1 and 0.
Protons and neutrons form the nucleus; electrons orbit the space around.
Equal numbers of electrons and protons keep the atom neutral.

concepts.title: Atomic Models: From Thomson to Rutherford
concepts.definition: Atomic models evolved by experiment: Thomson pictured electrons embedded in a positive sphere, but Rutherford's gold foil experiment scattered some alpha particles sharply, proving a tiny dense positive nucleus with electrons around it - and raising the stability puzzle that Bohr answered with fixed orbits.
concepts.key_idea: Experiments redraw the atom: scattering data forced the nucleus into the picture.
concepts.textbook_ref: iesc108.txt sections on Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr models
question_patterns: describe Thomson's model of the atom
what did the alpha particle scattering experiment reveal
state the postulates of Rutherford's model
what drawback of Rutherford's model did Bohr remove
compare Thomson and Rutherford models
why is the nucleus tiny compared to the atom

solution_steps.explain: Note what each scientist proposed and why.
Gold foil observations support a central nucleus.
Each model fixed the previous one's drawback.

concepts.title: Electron Arrangement in Shells
concepts.definition: Electrons occupy shells around the nucleus with fixed capacities - 2 in the K shell, 8 in the L, and so on by the 2 n squared rule - filling from the innermost shell outward; the outermost shell decides the atom's chemistry.
concepts.key_idea: Fill inner shells first: the outermost shell's electrons do the chemistry.
concepts.textbook_ref: iesc108.txt sections on shell arrangement and valence
question_patterns: write the electron arrangement of the given atom
how many electrons fit in the M shell
state the 2n squared rule with examples
why do electrons fill the K shell first
find the valence electrons of the given element from its arrangement
distribute the given number of electrons in shells

solution_steps.explain: The first shell holds at most 2 electrons.
Use the 2 n squared capacity, starting outward only after inner shells fill.
Its electron count gives the valency behaviour.
